The reproductive biology of the Spinifex hopping mouse reflects an arid-zone strategy of rapid and flexible output. Females produce litters averaging 3.9 pups [N_R_i = litters averaging 3.9 pups], and under favorable conditions following rainfall, they can initiate a new litter approximately every 33 days [F_R_i = litter approximately every 33 days], a remarkable frequency for a small murid rodent. This capacity for repeated breeding is supported by a brief gestation period of 35 days [tg = 35 days], which is reliably expressed when individuals are maintained at a core body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. The ability to sustain such rapid reproductive cycles is central to the species' persistence in an environment where breeding opportunities are unpredictable and often concentrated in brief pulses of resource abundance.

Neonatal development in this species begins from a very modest starting point, with pups weighing just 2.83 grams [Wwb = 2.83 grams] at birth. This altricial condition necessitates intensive maternal investment during the early postnatal period. The young grow rapidly while relying entirely on milk, and the transition to nutritional independence occurs relatively early. Weaning is completed by the time pups reach 30 days after birth [tx = 30 days after birth], a developmental milestone that, like gestation, depends on maintaining a stable maternal temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. At the point of weaning, the offspring typically attain a body mass of 12.5 grams [Wwx = 12.5 grams], representing more than a fourfold increase from their birth weight, reflecting the efficiency of maternal provisioning during the suckling period.

Sexual maturation proceeds swiftly in this desert-adapted rodent, allowing populations to capitalize on brief windows of favorable conditions. Females reach puberty at 75 days after birth [tp = 75 days after birth], a relatively rapid trajectory that is consistently observed when individuals are kept at an ambient temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This early onset of reproductive capability, combined with the female's ability to produce consecutive litters in quick succession, enables rapid population growth following significant rainfall events. The timing of puberty is closely aligned with the attainment of near-adult body mass, ensuring that females have accrued sufficient somatic resources to support the energetic demands of gestation and lactation.

Adult body size in Notomys alexis is modest even by the standards of its subfamily, with individuals reaching an ultimate wet weight of 35 grams [Wwi = 35 grams]. This relatively small size is characteristic of many desert-dwelling heteromyid and murid rodents, and it confers several thermoregulatory and energetic advantages. A smaller body reduces absolute metabolic water requirements and facilitates the use of shallow burrows for shelter. Despite its diminutive stature, the species exhibits a maximum recorded lifespan of 6.4 years [am = 6.4 years] under controlled captive conditions maintained at 38 °C [T = 38 °C]. This longevity, nearly twice that predicted by allometric equations for a rodent of its mass, underscores a life-history strategy that balances high reproductive output with a surprisingly extended reproductive window for a small mammal.

Comparative analyses with other Australian murids reveal that the life-history profile of the Spinifex hopping mouse is finely tuned to the variability of its habitat. The combination of a brief gestation of 35 days [tg = 35 days] at a body temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C] (matching the species' typical thermoneutral zone), and a rapid pubertal development of 75 days after birth [tp = 75 days after birth] under those same conditions, allows for multiple generations to be produced within a single productive season. When compared to other small Australian murids, this species' rapid pubertal development is notably swift, enabling a quick population turnover that is crucial for exploiting brief resource pulses. This extended lifespan, exceeding that of many similarly sized rodents, provides additional breeding opportunities across successive seasons.
